## Attribution

This lab is based on the workshop *Prompt, Run, Verify: Using LLMs for Data Analysis in Public Health* by Heather Mattie, Ph.D. (Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health). The dataset, the codebook, and the "Spot the bug" exercise come from her materials, available at <https://github.com/hmattie/Prompt-Run-Verify-Workshop>{target="_blank"}. We adapted the tasks to the coding agents and workflow used in this course.
:::

## Learning goals

- Tell apart numbers an LLM *typed* from numbers code *printed*.
- Find silent bugs in AI-generated code: code that runs cleanly and is wrong.
- Write a known-answer test *before* prompting, and make the agent's job "pass this test."
- Practice the no-upload workflow for data you cannot share: describe, fake, develop, run.
- Disclose and own your AI use.

## Lab description

Work in **pairs**. Use the agents you set up in Lab 00 (Codex, Claude, or Antigravity in VS Code); for Task 1 you will also want a plain chat window. Keep a record of **every prompt you send and a short note on what came back**, as in all our labs; this is part of the deliverable.

Submit a single Quarto document (`lab08.qmd`) and its rendered HTML through GitHub by Sunday, as usual. Whatever you do not finish in class, finish at home.

### Setup (before the session starts)

1. Download [`nhanes_workshop.csv`](nhanes_workshop.csv) into a new folder `lab08/` in your class repository.
2. Create `lab08.qmd` in the same folder. Load the data:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
dat <- read_csv("nhanes_workshop.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

3. Read the codebook below. **Do not** give it to the agent yet.

### Codebook

`nhanes_workshop.csv`: 1,000 adults aged 20 and older, a random sample from the public [`NHANES` R package](https://cran.r-project.org/package=NHANES) (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, 2009--2012). It is public data and safe to upload. For teaching, the data were changed in two ways that an LLM won't notice unless you tell it: missing BMI values are coded as 999, and race/ethnicity is stored as the numbers 1--5.

| Variable | Type | Description | Values or units | Missing coded as |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `study_id` | text | Participant ID (made up for the workshop) | P0001--P1000 | none |
| `age` | number | Age at screening | years, 20--80 (80 = 80 or older) | none |
| `sex` | text | Sex | `"female"` or `"male"` (lowercase) | none |
| `race` | integer, **categorical** | Race/ethnicity | 1 = White, 2 = Black, 3 = Mexican American, 4 = Other Hispanic, 5 = Other/Multiracial | none |
| `education` | text | Highest education completed | 8th Grade; 9 - 11th Grade; High School; Some College; College Grad | blank |
| `bmi` | number | Body mass index | kg/m² | **999** |
| `sbp` | number | Systolic blood pressure (average of readings) | mmHg | blank |
| `diabetes` | text | Ever told by a health professional they have diabetes | `"No"` or `"Yes"` | blank |
| `phys_active` | text | Does moderate or vigorous sports, fitness, or recreation | `"No"` or `"Yes"` | blank |
| `ever_smoker` | text | Smoked at least 100 cigarettes in lifetime | `"No"` or `"Yes"` | blank |

These are teaching data; don't use them for research or population estimates.

## How to use the prompts

Every grey box labeled with a prompt number (P1, P2, ...) is a complete prompt: hover over it, click the copy button in its top-right corner, and paste the whole box into the chat or agent in one go. Do not edit the wording unless a task says so; comparing answers only works if everybody sends the same prompt.

## Task 1: Ask your model for 20 decimals (5 minutes)

**Round 1.** Open a plain chat window (not your coding agent) and, if your model has a code execution option, turn it **off**. Paste this whole block:

```{.default}
P0a
Here are 25 systolic blood pressure readings:
130, 118, 100, 119, 96, 90, 120, 148, 114, 130, 99, 124, 131,
130, 148, 98, 118, 114, 113, 134, 116, 143, 158, 112, 110

Don't run any code or use any tools. Just tell me the mean and the sample
standard deviation, both to 20 decimal places.
```

**Round 2.** Start a new chat with code execution **on**, and paste this whole block:

```{.default}
P0b
Here are 25 systolic blood pressure readings:
130, 118, 100, 119, 96, 90, 120, 148, 114, 130, 99, 124, 131,
130, 148, 98, 118, 114, 113, 134, 116, 143, 158, 112, 110

Calculate the mean and the sample standard deviation, both to 20 decimal
places. Show me the exact code you ran and tell me which language it was in.
```

In your document, record the model's name and both answers. Then compare them, digit by digit, with the exact values:

| Statistic | Exact value to 20 decimal places |
|---|---|
| Mean | 120.52000000000000000000 |
| Sample SD | 17.41436188896969029564 |

For each answer, at which decimal does it first go wrong? Finally, run this in R and do the same comparison:

```{r}
#| label: task1-check
#| eval: false
x <- c(130, 118, 100, 119, 96, 90, 120, 148, 114, 130, 99, 124, 131,
       130, 148, 98, 118, 114, 113, 134, 116, 143, 158, 112, 110)
sprintf("%.20f", mean(x))
sprintf("%.20f", sd(x))
```

Why does R also get the SD wrong after a certain decimal? If the code-on chat got all 20 decimals right, what in its code made that possible?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: getting more than 15 decimals in R

R stores numbers as doubles, which hold about 15 to 16 **significant digits**. The SD has two digits before the decimal point, so R runs out of precision after about the 15th decimal. `options(digits = 22)` and `sprintf("%.20f", ...)` do not help: they print more digits but do not compute more, so the extra digits carry no information.

To compute more digits you need arbitrary-precision arithmetic. In R, the [`Rmpfr`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=Rmpfr){target="_blank"} package does this. Convert your numbers with `mpfr()` and choose a precision in bits; `mean()`, `sum()`, and `sqrt()` then work as usual. Try it with `precBits = 128` and compare with the exact values above.
:::

## Task 2: Spot the bug (12 minutes)

Each chunk below is code an LLM wrote from a prompt that did **not** include the codebook. All four have a problem. Only one of them tells you so.

**First, without AI.** Paste each chunk into `lab08.qmd`, run it, and answer with your partner:

1. Did R (or the compiler) complain?
2. Is the result **plausible**? Check the number of people, the values, and the number of estimates.
3. What would you change, **in the code or in the prompt**?

**Then, with AI.** Once you have your own answers, paste prompts P-A to P-D into your VS Code agent (with `lab08/` open, so it can run the R code on the CSV). Did it find the silent ones?

### Bug A

> **Original prompt:** "Make a scatterplot of BMI vs. systolic blood pressure with a trend line."

```{r}
#| label: bug-a
#| eval: false
dat %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bmi, y = sbp)) %>%
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) %>%
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

```{.default}
P-A
The file nhanes_workshop.csv in this folder is read into R with
dat <- readr::read_csv("nhanes_workshop.csv"). An LLM wrote the code below
for the request "Make a scatterplot of BMI vs. systolic blood pressure with a
trend line." Run it. Is anything wrong with this code or its output?

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
dat %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bmi, y = sbp)) %>%
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) %>%
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

### Bug B

> **Original prompt:** "Fit a linear regression of systolic BP on BMI, age, sex, and race."

```{r}
#| label: bug-b
#| eval: false
fit <- lm(sbp ~ bmi + age + sex + race, data = dat)
summary(fit)$coefficients %>% round(3)
```

```{.default}
P-B
The file nhanes_workshop.csv in this folder is read into R with
dat <- readr::read_csv("nhanes_workshop.csv"). An LLM wrote the code below
for the request "Fit a linear regression of systolic BP on BMI, age, sex, and
race." Run it. Is anything wrong with this code or its output?

library(dplyr)
fit <- lm(sbp ~ bmi + age + sex + race, data = dat)
summary(fit)$coefficients %>% round(3)
```

### Bug C

> **Original prompt:** "What is the mean systolic blood pressure for women?"

```{r}
#| label: bug-c
#| eval: false
dat %>%
  filter(sex == "Female") %>%
  summarize(n = n(), mean_sbp = mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{.default}
P-C
The file nhanes_workshop.csv in this folder is read into R with
dat <- readr::read_csv("nhanes_workshop.csv"). An LLM wrote the code below
for the request "What is the mean systolic blood pressure for women?" Run it.
Is anything wrong with this code or its output?

library(dplyr)
dat %>%
  filter(sex == "Female") %>%
  summarize(n = n(), mean_sbp = mean(sbp, na.rm = TRUE))
```

### Bug D

> **Original prompt:** "Write a `factorial` function in C++ for my `Binom` class from Lab 05."

Save this as `factorial.cpp`, then compile and run it with `g++ -std=c++14 -Wall factorial.cpp -o factorial && ./factorial`. Compare with `factorial(10:14)` in R.

```cpp
#include <iostream>

int factorial(int k) {
  int ans = 1;
  for (int i = 2; i <= k; ++i) ans *= i;
  return ans;
}

int main() {
  for (int k = 10; k <= 14; ++k)
    std::cout << k << "! = " << factorial(k) << std::endl;
  return 0;
}
```

```{.default}
P-D
An LLM wrote the C++ function below for the request "Write a factorial
function in C++ for my Binom class." It compiles without warnings with
g++ -std=c++14 -Wall. Is anything wrong with it?

int factorial(int k) {
  int ans = 1;
  for (int i = 2; i <= k; ++i) ans *= i;
  return ans;
}
```

**Discuss:** Which of the four is the most difficult to spot?

## Task 3: Prompt, run, verify (13 minutes)

Now do the opening regression from the lecture properly, with your agent, and verify each step. Use **one** chat for P1, P2, and P3, in that order.

### Round 1: without the codebook

Open `lab08/` in VS Code and paste this into your agent:

```{.default}
P1
There is a CSV in this folder with data on US adults. Give me an overview of
the variables, their types, and any values that look unusual. Then write the R
code to do the same check myself, in a chunk I can paste into lab08.qmd.
```

Before reading the agent's answer, run the code it gave you and look at the output yourself. Then compare:

- Did the agent notice that `race` is stored as a number? That `bmi` has a maximum of 999?
- Did it *type* any numbers (a mean, a count) that differ from what the code printed?

### Round 2: with the codebook

```{.default}
P2
The codebook says: bmi = 999 means missing. race is a categorical variable
coded 1 = White, 2 = Black, 3 = Mexican American, 4 = Other Hispanic,
5 = Other/Multiracial. sex is "female"/"male", lowercase.

Clean the data accordingly. Then fit a linear regression of systolic BP (sbp)
on BMI, age, sex, and race/ethnicity, and show the coefficient table with 95%
confidence intervals. Give me the R code, with comments, in one chunk.
```

### Verify

Run the five checks from the lecture and write one line per check in your document:

1. **Runs cleanly.** Any warnings? Any "Removed N rows" messages?
2. **Right shape.** How many rows in `dat`? How many people in the model (`nobs(fit)`)? Where did the difference go?
3. **Plausible values.** `summary(dat$bmi)` after cleaning. Does the race table have five levels with sensible counts?
4. **Known answer.** How many coefficient rows should a categorical `race` with 5 levels produce? Does it?
5. **Right question.** The data are cross-sectional. Paste P3, then read the summary looking for "significant", "causes", "reduces", or "risk". Would you keep its wording?

```{.default}
P3
Write a two-sentence summary of these regression results for the Results
section of a public health manuscript.
```

Finally, compare the coefficient table with the one from Bug B in Task 2. What changed, and why?

## Task 4: The no-upload workflow, test first (13 minutes)

Pretend `nhanes_workshop.csv` is an EHR extract with protected health information. It cannot go in a chat, and a cloud agent must not read it.

Your goal is a function, `mean_sbp_by_group(dat, group)`, that returns, for each level of `group`, the number of people, the number of missing `sbp` values, and the mean `sbp` among the non-missing.

### Step 0: set up a clean folder and write the test, by hand

1. Create a folder `lab08-noupload/` **outside your class repository**, for example on your Desktop, with no data in it. Do not put it next to `lab08/`: an agent can see everything in the folder that is open, including sibling folders when the whole repository is open.
2. Open it in a **new VS Code window** (File > New Window, then File > Open Folder). Do not add it to your existing workspace with "Add Folder to Workspace"; a multi-root workspace lets the agent see both folders.
3. Open your agent's chat panel in that new window. This is the only folder the agent should work in for this task.
4. Without AI, save the following as `test-mean-sbp.R` in that folder. Then add **at least one more check** of your own at the bottom. Think about what could go wrong silently: what should happen to a group with *all* `sbp` missing? To a `group` column that is numeric?

```{r}
#| label: known-answer
#| eval: false
# test-mean-sbp.R: known-answer test for mean_sbp_by_group()
source("mean-sbp.R")

test <- data.frame(
  sex = c("female", "female", "female", "male", "male", "male"),
  sbp = c(120, 130, NA, 140, 150, 160)
)
# Expected by hand: female -> n = 3, missing = 1, mean = 125
#                   male   -> n = 3, missing = 0, mean = 150

res <- mean_sbp_by_group(test, "sex")
stopifnot(
  nrow(res) == 2,
  res$n[res$sex == "female"] == 3,
  res$n_missing[res$sex == "female"] == 1,
  isTRUE(all.equal(res$mean_sbp[res$sex == "female"], 125)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(res$mean_sbp[res$sex == "male"], 150))
)

# Your additional check(s) here

cat("All tests passed\n")
```

### Step 1: describe, don't upload

In the chat panel of the `lab08-noupload/` window, paste this whole block. It describes the data's structure only, never its rows. The prompt asks the agent to run your test with `Rscript`, so **approve** the agent's request to run that command when it asks; otherwise it will write the code and stop without testing it. If the agent reports that `Rscript` is not found (common on Windows), tell it the full path, for example `"C:\Program Files\R\R-4.5.1\bin\Rscript.exe"`, or run the test yourself in the R console with `source("test-mean-sbp.R")` and paste the output back.

```{.default}
P4
Context: I'm working in R with dplyr. My data frame `dat` has 1,000 rows. I
can't share the data because of privacy rules. Its columns are:
- study_id (character, "P0001" to "P1000")
- age (numeric, years, 20 to 80; no missing)
- sex (character, "female" or "male", lowercase; no missing)
- race (integer 1 to 5, categorical: 1 = White, 2 = Black, 3 = Mexican
  American, 4 = Other Hispanic, 5 = Other/Multiracial; no missing)
- education (character: "8th Grade", "9 - 11th Grade", "High School",
  "Some College", "College Grad"; missing is blank)
- bmi (numeric, kg/m2; missing is coded as 999)
- sbp (numeric, systolic blood pressure in mmHg; missing is NA)
- diabetes, phys_active, ever_smoker (character, "No" or "Yes"; missing is NA)

Objective: a function mean_sbp_by_group(dat, group), where group is the name
of a column as a string. For each level of that column it returns a data
frame with the group column, n (number of people), n_missing (number of
missing sbp), and mean_sbp (mean sbp among non-missing values).

Format: Two files in this folder. First, fake-data.R, which creates a 50-row
fake data frame `dat` with exactly this structure, including a few 999s in
bmi and a few NAs in sbp. Second, mean-sbp.R, which defines
mean_sbp_by_group() with comments. Do not edit test-mean-sbp.R. Then run
Rscript test-mean-sbp.R and keep fixing mean-sbp.R until it prints
"All tests passed". Tell me how many attempts it took.
```

### Step 2: develop on fake data

Check the agent's work yourself: run `fake-data.R` and look at the fake data (does it have 999s and lowercase `sex`?), then run `test-mean-sbp.R`. Did the agent edit your test file even though you told it not to? Record how many attempts it reported.

### Step 3: run on the real data

Copy `mean-sbp.R`, `fake-data.R`, and `test-mean-sbp.R` into `lab08/` (the "approved environment" where the data live, and the folder you submit), then paste this chunk into `lab08.qmd`:

```{r}
#| label: real-data
#| eval: false
source("mean-sbp.R")
dat <- readr::read_csv("nhanes_workshop.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    bmi  = na_if(bmi, 999),
    race = factor(race, levels = 1:5,
                  labels = c("White", "Black", "Mexican American",
                             "Other Hispanic", "Other/Multiracial"))
  )
mean_sbp_by_group(dat, "sex")
mean_sbp_by_group(dat, "race")
```

Does the `sex` result match what you found in Task 3 and in Bug C?
